title: State & Data Flow in SwiftUI
scopeHtml: Scope: @State, @Binding, @Observable, @Bindable, @Environment, @AppStorage, source of truth, ObservableObject legacy, state hoisting comparison.

notes.title: Baseline and source of truth
notes.html:
Baseline. Swift 6 language mode, Xcode 16+, iOS 17/18 minimum, SwiftUI-first. We teach @Observable (Observation framework, iOS 17+) first. ObservableObject, @Published, @StateObject, @ObservedObject appear only labelled "old codebases". Fast-moving details are marked verify.

Android equivalent first. In Compose, the rule is "state flows down, events flow up" (state hoisting): a stateless composable gets value and onValueChange, and a ViewModel or a parent owns the state. SwiftUI uses the same principle with different tools: the source of truth is owned by exactly one place (@State in a view, or an @Observable model), and everything else holds a reference or binding to it, never a copy.

Languages: Swift · Kotlin
// Owner holds truth; child gets a Binding (read + write)
struct Parent: View {
    @State private var name = ""
    var body: some View {
        NameField(name: $name)
        Text("Hi, \(name)")
    }
}

struct NameField: View {
    @Binding var name: String
    var body: some View { TextField("Name", text: $name) }
}
@Composable
fun Parent() {
    var name by remember { mutableStateOf("") }
    NameField(name = name, onNameChange = { name = it })
    Text("Hi, $name")
}

@Composable
fun NameField(name: String, onNameChange: (String) -> Unit) {
    TextField(value = name, onValueChange = onNameChange)
}

The big difference. Compose hoists with a value plus a callback; SwiftUI bundles both into a Binding<Value>, a two-way reference (getter and setter closures). The single-source-of-truth discipline is the same: never keep two independent copies of the same data.

Concern Compose / Android SwiftUI
Local UI state remember { mutableStateOf() } @State
Survive rotation / process death rememberSaveable, SavedStateHandle rotation is not a recreate; @SceneStorage for restoration
Two-way parameter value + lambda @Binding
Screen-level state holder ViewModel + StateFlow @Observable class (often @MainActor)
Read ViewModel in UI collectAsStateWithLifecycle() just read properties; tracking is automatic
App-wide dependencies Hilt / CompositionLocal @Environment
Preferences DataStore / SharedPreferences @AppStorage (UserDefaults)

Decision ladder (which wrapper do I use?).

  1. Simple value owned by this view only: @State.
  2. Child needs to read and write a parent's value: @Binding.
  3. Reference-type model (many properties, logic, async): @Observable class; the view that creates it stores it in @State; others receive it as a plain let/var parameter, or as @Bindable when they need $ bindings to its properties.
  4. Shared across many distant views (theme, router, current user): @Environment.
  5. Persisted small user settings: @AppStorage. Per-scene UI restoration: @SceneStorage.

Real industry examples. Apple's own sample apps (Fruta, Backyard Birds, Food Truck) follow exactly this ladder. TCA (Swift Composable Architecture) takes it further with one Store as truth and scoped child stores, much like a single Redux/MVI state tree on Android.

Everyday analogy. The source of truth is the original deed to a house. A Binding is a signed power of attorney to act on it; a copy of the deed is a forged duplicate that goes out of date.

Common interview traps.

  • Keeping a local @State copy of a parent's value (the copy goes stale or fights the parent).
  • Saying @Binding stores data; it only references data owned elsewhere.
  • Android vs iOS: there is no onValueChange boilerplate, but there is also no automatic ViewModel survival; view models live as long as the view that owns them (see the lifecycle section).

notes.title: @State and @Binding
notes.html:
Android equivalent first. @State is remember { mutableStateOf(...) } and @Binding is the hoisted (value, onValueChange) pair squashed into one parameter.

struct CounterView: View {
    @State private var count = 0           // owned here

    var body: some View {
        VStack {
            Text("Count: \(count)")
            Button("Add") { count += 1 }
            StepperRow(value: $count)      // $count is a Binding<Int>
        }
    }
}

struct StepperRow: View {
    @Binding var value: Int
    var body: some View { Stepper("Value \(value)", value: $value) }
}

How @State actually works.

  • The view struct is recreated constantly, so it cannot hold mutable data. @State stores its value in SwiftUI-managed storage outside the struct, attached to the view's identity (position/.id in the tree). The property wrapper is just a handle to that storage.
  • The initial value in @State private var count = 0 is used only the first time the view with that identity appears. Later re-creations of the struct reuse the stored value and ignore the initialiser expression.
  • Writing to @State marks the view's dependent body invalid, scheduling a new evaluation on the next run-loop turn.
  • Mark @State private; it is local, owned data. Apple's guidance: never pass @State as a plain value expecting two-way sync; pass $state.

Passing the wrong thing. StepperRow(value: count) fails to compile (expects Binding<Int>); StepperRow(value: .constant(3)) is a read-only binding used in previews. Create custom bindings when transforming data:

Languages: Swift · Kotlin
Toggle("Enabled", isOn: Binding(
    get: { settings.level > 0 },
    set: { settings.level = $0 ? 1 : 0 }
))
Switch(
    checked = settings.level > 0,
    onCheckedChange = { settings.level = if (it) 1 else 0 }
)

Initialising @State from a parameter. This is a classic trap:

struct EditView: View {
    @State private var draft: String
    init(initial: String) {
        _draft = State(initialValue: initial)   // sets only the FIRST value
    }
    var body: some View { TextField("Edit", text: $draft) }
}

If the parent later passes a different initial for the same identity, draft does not reset. To reset, give the view a new identity (.id(item.id)) or use onChange(of:). Compose has the same trap: remember(key) is needed to reset.

@State for value types with copy semantics. For structs, mutation (user.name = "A") replaces the whole value and triggers an update. For arrays, each append changes the array value. For classes, @State only notices reassigning the reference, not mutating its properties (unless it is @Observable, see below). This is the most common beginner bug.

@Binding details.

  • $x on @State gives Binding<T>; on an @Bindable model gives bindings to its properties; $array[i], $user.address.city derive sub-bindings via key paths. ForEach($items) { $item in ... } (iOS 15+) gives a binding per element, convenient for editing rows.
  • A binding is a pair of closures plus a transaction; it keeps the source alive only via the owner. It is not thread-safe: change it on the main actor.

Real industry examples. Form-heavy screens (checkout, profile edit) use a draft @State copy that is committed on Save and discarded on Cancel; this is the iOS idiom for "editing a copy" (Compose: a local remember draft).

Everyday analogy. @State is the whiteboard in your own office; @Binding is a window into the whiteboard of the office next door, letting you read and write with the owner's permission.

Common interview traps.

  • Mutating an object stored in @State and expecting a refresh when it is a plain class.
  • Expecting @State's initial value to be re-applied when parameters change.
  • Making @State non-private and writing to it from outside the view's body flow.
  • Android vs iOS: @State survives parent recomposition like remember, but is lost when the view leaves the tree (not rotation, which does not exist as a recreate in SwiftUI).

notes.title: @Observable versus ObservableObject
notes.html:
Android equivalent first. On Android, a ViewModel exposes StateFlow<UiState> and the composable collects it. In SwiftUI the model is an @Observable class and views just read properties; SwiftUI records which properties each view's body reads and re-evaluates the view when those change.

Languages: Swift · Kotlin
import Observation

@MainActor
@Observable
final class CartModel {
    var items: [CartItem] = []
    var isLoading = false
    var errorMessage: String?

    var total: Decimal { items.reduce(0) { $0 + $1.price } }

    func load() async {
        isLoading = true
        defer { isLoading = false }
        do { items = try await CartService.shared.fetch() }
        catch { errorMessage = error.localizedDescription }
    }
}

struct CartScreen: View {
    @State private var model = CartModel()    // creator owns it

    var body: some View {
        List(model.items) { Text($0.name) }
            .overlay { if model.isLoading { ProgressView() } }
            .task { await model.load() }
    }
}
@HiltViewModel
class CartViewModel @Inject constructor(private val service: CartService) : ViewModel() {
    private val _state = MutableStateFlow(CartState())
    val state = _state.asStateFlow()

    fun load() = viewModelScope.launch {
        _state.update { it.copy(isLoading = true) }
        runCatching { service.fetch() }
            .onSuccess { items -> _state.update { it.copy(items = items, isLoading = false) } }
            .onFailure { e -> _state.update { it.copy(errorMessage = e.message, isLoading = false) } }
    }
}

@Composable
fun CartScreen(vm: CartViewModel = hiltViewModel()) {
    val state by vm.state.collectAsStateWithLifecycle()
    LazyColumn { items(state.items) { Text(it.name) } }
}

What the @Observable macro does (iOS 17+). It rewrites each stored property into a computed property backed by a hidden _name storage, adding calls to an ObservationRegistrar: access(keyPath:) on read and withMutation(keyPath:) on write. During body evaluation SwiftUI runs withObservationTracking, which records every property read; when one of those properties changes, only the views that read it are invalidated. Unread properties never trigger updates. @ObservationIgnored opts a property out (caches, dependencies you do not want tracked).

The legacy form you will meet in old codebases (pre-iOS 17).

final class CartModel: ObservableObject {
    @Published var items: [CartItem] = []
    @Published var isLoading = false
}

struct CartScreen: View {
    @StateObject private var model = CartModel()      // creator owns lifetime
    var body: some View { ChildView(model: model) }
}
struct ChildView: View {
    @ObservedObject var model: CartModel              // does NOT own lifetime
    var body: some View { Text("\(model.items.count)") }
}
Aspect ObservableObject (legacy) @Observable (iOS 17+)
Granularity Any @Published change invalidates every view observing the object Only views that read the changed property
Wrapper in owning view @StateObject @State
Wrapper in child @ObservedObject / @EnvironmentObject plain property, @Bindable, @Environment
Optional / collection support clumsy works with optionals and nested @Observable
Backed by Combine (objectWillChange) Observation, no Combine
Back-deployment iOS 13+ iOS 17+ (there is an open-source back-port ecosystem, e.g. Perception in Point-Free; verify before relying)

Over-invalidation example. With ObservableObject, a row showing model.name re-renders when an unrelated isLoading flips. With @Observable it does not. This is the main performance reason to migrate and is what interviewers want to hear.

Concurrency notes (Swift 6). Mark view models @MainActor so UI state is mutated only on the main actor; async work inside runs in await calls that hop off and back on automatically. In Swift 6 mode, a non-Sendable model captured in a Task from a nonisolated context is a hard error; @MainActor @Observable classes are implicitly Sendable.

Real industry examples. Apple's sample projects migrated to @Observable in 2023-2024. Teams at large apps mix both while migrating; Point-Free's swift-perception backports observation-style tracking to older iOS versions (verify current status).

Everyday analogy. ObservableObject is a shop bell that rings for every customer whenever anything on the shelf changes. @Observable is a bell that only rings for customers who asked about that exact item.

Common interview traps.

  • Using @StateObject with an @Observable class (wrong wrapper, compile error or wrong lifetime). Use @State.
  • Forgetting that @Observable classes must be reference types; a struct will not work.
  • Marking a property @Published inside an @Observable class (ignored/redundant).
  • Android vs iOS: you don't "collect" or "subscribe"; reading in body is the subscription. Reading properties outside body (in init or a closure that runs later) is not tracked.

notes.title: @Bindable, @Environment and custom keys
notes.html:
Android equivalent first. Compose's CompositionLocal / Hilt injection pass shared things implicitly down the tree. SwiftUI's @Environment is the same: values flow to all descendants without being threaded through initialisers.

@Bindable. @Observable classes do not give you $ bindings automatically. @Bindable creates them:

struct ProfileEditor: View {
    @Bindable var profile: ProfileModel            // @Observable class passed in

    var body: some View {
        Form {
            TextField("Name", text: $profile.name)
            Toggle("Public", isOn: $profile.isPublic)
        }
    }
}

You can also write @Bindable var model = model inside body for an object obtained from the environment. Use @Bindable only when you need bindings; for read-only use a plain let.

@Environment for system values. @Environment(\.colorScheme), \.dismiss, \.horizontalSizeClass, \.openURL, \.scenePhase, \.modelContext (SwiftData), \.locale, \.dynamicTypeSize. Reading scenePhase is how SwiftUI tells you about active/inactive/background (see lifecycle section).

@Environment for your own @Observable objects (iOS 17+).

@main
struct ShopApp: App {
    @State private var session = SessionModel()

    var body: some Scene {
        WindowGroup {
            RootView()
                .environment(session)          // inject by type
        }
    }
}

struct AccountBadge: View {
    @Environment(SessionModel.self) private var session   // crashes if not injected
    var body: some View { Text(session.user?.name ?? "Guest") }
}

If a view reads @Environment(SessionModel.self) and no ancestor injected it, the app crashes at runtime ("No Observable object of type SessionModel found", a classic crash signature). Use optionals: @Environment(SessionModel.self) private var session: SessionModel? (supported; verify for your SDK).

Legacy @EnvironmentObject. Old code does .environmentObject(model) and @EnvironmentObject var model: Model for ObservableObject types; same crash if missing.

Custom environment keys (values, not objects). Use the @Entry macro in newer SDKs (Xcode 16, back-deploys; verify) or the classic key:

Languages: Swift · Kotlin
// Xcode 16+ (verify)
extension EnvironmentValues {
    @Entry var analytics: AnalyticsClient = .noop
}

// Classic form (still common)
private struct ThemeKey: EnvironmentKey {
    static let defaultValue = Theme.standard      // static let: Swift 6 safe
}
extension EnvironmentValues {
    var theme: Theme {
        get { self[ThemeKey.self] }
        set { self[ThemeKey.self] = newValue }
    }
}
// use: .environment(\.theme, .dark) and @Environment(\.theme) var theme
val LocalAnalytics = staticCompositionLocalOf<AnalyticsClient> { NoopAnalytics }

CompositionLocalProvider(LocalAnalytics provides realAnalytics) {
    RootScreen()
}
// use: val analytics = LocalAnalytics.current

Environment as dependency injection. Putting protocols or clients (API client, analytics, image loader, feature flags) into the environment gives testable previews: override with fakes in #Preview or tests. For larger apps, libraries like Point-Free's swift-dependencies (@Dependency) or Factory/Swinject provide DI containers, similar to Hilt/Koin on Android.

Cost. Environment values propagate down; changing one value invalidates the views that read that key. Avoid putting rapidly changing values (scroll offset) into the environment.

Real industry examples. Apple apps use the environment for modelContext and dismiss. Airbnb-style design systems pass theme and spacing tokens through the environment.

Everyday analogy. The environment is the building's wiring: any room can plug in without a cable running through every corridor, but if the outlet is not installed, the lamp stays dark (crash).

Common interview traps.

  • Forgetting to inject an environment object on a sheet or popover root in legacy code (sheets inherited it in most cases, but a new UIHostingController does not).
  • Using @Bindable when a plain parameter would do, or forgetting it and getting "cannot find $ in scope".
  • Mutable static var defaultValue for keys under Swift 6.
  • Android vs iOS: CompositionLocal has staticCompositionLocalOf vs compositionLocalOf performance semantics; SwiftUI has no such split, but reads are tracked per key.

notes.title: AppStorage and SceneStorage
notes.html:
Android equivalent first. Android persists small settings with DataStore (or SharedPreferences) and restores UI state with rememberSaveable / SavedStateHandle. SwiftUI offers @AppStorage for UserDefaults and @SceneStorage for per-scene restoration.

Languages: Swift · Kotlin
struct SettingsView: View {
    @AppStorage("isDarkOverride") private var darkOverride = false
    @AppStorage("fontScale") private var fontScale = 1.0
    @AppStorage("lastTab") private var lastTab: Tab = .home      // RawRepresentable String/Int enum

    var body: some View {
        Form {
            Toggle("Force dark", isOn: $darkOverride)
            Slider(value: $fontScale, in: 0.8...1.4)
        }
    }
}
val Context.dataStore by preferencesDataStore("settings")
val DARK = booleanPreferencesKey("isDarkOverride")

@Composable
fun SettingsView(context: Context) {
    val scope = rememberCoroutineScope()
    val dark by context.dataStore.data.map { it[DARK] ?: false }.collectAsState(false)
    Switch(dark, { v -> scope.launch { context.dataStore.edit { it[DARK] = v } } })
}

@AppStorage facts.

  • Backed by UserDefaults.standard (or a suite via store:). Supported types: Bool, Int, Double, String, URL, Data, and RawRepresentable enums whose raw value is Int or String. Optionals are supported for those types.
  • Writes publish a change so all views using the same key update, including across views you did not wire together.
  • It is synchronous, fine for small values. Do not store large JSON, tokens or secrets. Secrets go in the Keychain; large data in files/SwiftData.
  • App Groups: @AppStorage("k", store: UserDefaults(suiteName: "group.com.acme")) shares settings with widgets and extensions. Widgets cannot read your app's standard defaults without an App Group.
  • Not Sendable-friendly outside the main actor use; read it in views and pass values into models.

@SceneStorage facts.

  • Stores small values (same type set as AppStorage) per scene, used for state restoration: selected tab, scroll anchor id, draft text, expanded section. The system saves/restores it across app relaunches and when a scene is disconnected and reconnected; it is not a database and the system may discard it (do not rely on it for data).
  • iPad multi-window gives each window independent values, which @AppStorage cannot.
struct RootView: View {
    @SceneStorage("selectedTab") private var selectedTab = "home"
    @SceneStorage("draft") private var draft = ""
    var body: some View {
        TabView(selection: $selectedTab) {
            HomeView().tag("home").tabItem { Label("Home", systemImage: "house") }
            ComposeView(draft: $draft).tag("compose").tabItem { Label("New", systemImage: "square.and.pencil") }
        }
    }
}
Need Use
App-wide small preference @AppStorage
Per-window UI restoration @SceneStorage
Secrets, tokens Keychain
Structured/large local data SwiftData (or Core Data/GRDB in old code)
Share with extension/widget @AppStorage + App Group suite, or shared SwiftData container

Production incident patterns. Storing an auth token in UserDefaults fails security review (plist readable on jailbroken or backed-up devices); keys typo'd as string literals in two files diverge silently, so centralise keys in a constant namespace; changing the enum raw value in an update makes @AppStorage fall back to the default.

Real industry examples. Apps persist theme choice, onboarding-seen flags and last-used tab in @AppStorage; Apple Notes-like apps use scene storage for draft restoration; widgets (Weather, custom apps) share App Group defaults.

Everyday analogy. @AppStorage is the sticky notes on your fridge everyone in the house sees; @SceneStorage is the bookmark in the book you left open on your own desk.

Common interview traps.

  • Storing sensitive data or large blobs in @AppStorage.
  • Treating @SceneStorage as persistent storage.
  • Expecting a widget to see standard UserDefaults without an App Group.
  • Android vs iOS: UserDefaults is synchronous and in-process; there is no Flow, the wrapper does the observation for views only.

notes.title: How SwiftUI tracks dependencies and re-renders
notes.html:
Android equivalent first. Compose tracks which State objects are read inside each recomposition scope with a snapshot system, then re-runs only those scopes. SwiftUI keeps a similar graph, called the attribute graph, but the unit is the view's body, not a lambda.

The pipeline.

state change (@State write / @Observable property write / Environment change)
        |
        v
mark dependent attribute(s) in the AttributeGraph as invalid
        |
        v
next transaction (run-loop turn): re-evaluate body of invalidated views
        |
        v
diff the new view tree against the old (by identity + value comparison)
        |
        v
update render tree / Core Animation layers only where output changed

What a view depends on. Anything read during body: its own @State, bindings, @Environment keys read, @Observable properties actually accessed, and its own stored properties (its inputs). When the parent re-evaluates and builds your struct again with equal inputs, SwiftUI can skip your body if it can prove equality (it compares stored properties field by field; for Equatable views it can use == with .equatable()). Closures are not comparable, so a view that stores a closure input is re-evaluated whenever the parent re-evaluates (a subtle perf cost; mitigate by passing values plus IDs, or by using @Observable with methods).

Observation tracking detail.

@Observable final class Model { var a = 0; var b = 0 }

struct V: View {
    let model: Model
    var body: some View {
        Text("\(model.a)")      // body reads `a` only
    }
}

Changing model.b does not re-evaluate V. Changing model.a does. Reading a property conditionally means the dependency set can change from run to run (tracked each time).

Re-evaluation is not the same as re-rendering. body re-evaluation produces a new tree of descriptions; the diff determines whether anything visible changes. Cheap bodies re-run often; expensive bodies must be avoided because they are on the main thread.

Debugging tools.

  • let _ = Self._printChanges() as the first line in body prints which property caused the evaluation (e.g. @self changed, _count changed). Undocumented, debug-only.
  • Instruments > SwiftUI template: View Body counts, "Cause & Effect" graph in newer Xcodes (verify Xcode 26 name/availability).
  • Breakpoints on body or didSet equivalents; in @Observable use withObservationTracking in tests to assert what is accessed.

Transactions and animation. Each state change is in a Transaction that can carry an animation. withAnimation sets the transaction's animation; .transaction { $0.animation = nil } disables animation for a subtree (e.g. while scrolling).

Threading. UI updates must happen on the main actor. Mutating @State or an @Observable property that views read from a background thread produces undefined behaviour and, in Swift 6 mode, usually a compile-time isolation error. Use @MainActor models and await MainActor.run {} only when truly needed.

Real industry examples. Apple's "Demystify SwiftUI" and "Discover Observation in SwiftUI" WWDC talks describe exactly this. Teams profiling large SwiftUI apps at Airbnb and Lyft discuss reducing body invalidations by splitting views and narrowing inputs.

Everyday analogy. The attribute graph is a spreadsheet: change one cell, only cells whose formulas reference it are recomputed.

Common interview traps.

  • Believing that any state change re-renders the whole screen.
  • Believing body is only called when visible output changes; it is called when a dependency changes, even if the result is identical.
  • Passing closures as inputs and wondering why children never get skipped.
  • Android vs iOS: Compose can skip a restartable function with stable params; SwiftUI compares stored properties, and closures break that.

notes.title: Lifecycle: when state is created and lost
notes.html:
Android equivalent first. Android ViewModels survive rotation via ViewModelStore and die when the screen is removed; remember dies on leaving composition or config change unless rememberSaveable. In SwiftUI, there is no configuration-change recreate; state lives and dies with view identity.

view appears at position/id P  -> @State storage allocated (initial value used once)
parent re-evaluates            -> struct recreated, storage reused (same identity)
view removed from tree / id changes -> storage destroyed

Where to create a model.

  • @State private var model = FeedModel() in the view that owns the screen. Since iOS 17 SwiftUI keeps the object created by the first @State initialiser, though the initialiser expression itself may be evaluated on every parent re-evaluation and the result discarded (an issue if FeedModel.init is heavy or has side effects). Defer work to .task, not init.
  • Legacy @StateObject solved this with an autoclosure; @ObservedObject created in the view (@ObservedObject var m = Model()) is a notorious bug source: the model is recreated each time the parent re-evaluates.
  • App-lifetime singletons belong in the App struct's @State and are injected via .environment.

Lifecycle hooks.

Android SwiftUI
LaunchedEffect(Unit) .task { } (auto-cancelled on disappear)
LaunchedEffect(key) .task(id: key) { }
DisposableEffect(onDispose) .onDisappear { } / cancel in deinit of owned object
onResume/onPause @Environment(\.scenePhase) .active / .background
snapshotFlow + collect .onChange(of: value) { old, new in } (iOS 17 two-parameter form)
Activity.onSaveInstanceState @SceneStorage, app delegate/scene state restoration
Languages: Swift · Kotlin
struct FeedScreen: View {
    @State private var model = FeedModel()
    @Environment(\.scenePhase) private var phase

    var body: some View {
        FeedList(model: model)
            .task { await model.refresh() }                 // cancelled when view disappears
            .onChange(of: phase) { _, new in
                if new == .active { Task { await model.refreshIfStale() } }
            }
    }
}
@Composable
fun FeedScreen(vm: FeedViewModel = hiltViewModel()) {
    LaunchedEffect(Unit) { vm.refresh() }
    val lifecycle = LocalLifecycleOwner.current.lifecycle
    DisposableEffect(lifecycle) {
        val obs = LifecycleEventObserver { _, e -> if (e == Lifecycle.Event.ON_RESUME) vm.refreshIfStale() }
        lifecycle.addObserver(obs); onDispose { lifecycle.removeObserver(obs) }
    }
}

onAppear vs task. .onAppear runs synchronously each time the view appears (may be repeated when navigating back or when lazy containers recreate rows). .task starts an async task at appear and cancels it at disappear, which is the safe default for loading data. Inside a TabView or NavigationStack, a view's onAppear may fire again when returning; make loads idempotent.

Navigation interplay. A view pushed on NavigationStack keeps its @State while it stays on the stack; popping destroys it. TabView tabs generally keep their state when switching (they remain in the tree), but a tab's content closure is re-evaluated; sheets and fullScreenCover create fresh state each presentation. Detailed navigation is in the next notes in this track.

Restoration after process death. iOS may kill a backgrounded app; the next launch is a cold start. Only @SceneStorage and your own persistence survive. Do not assume a ViewModel's in-memory data is there.

Real industry examples. Banking apps clear sensitive state on .background; media apps pause playback via scenePhase; news apps refresh on .active when data is older than N minutes.

Everyday analogy. @State is a plant bound to its pot (identity): move the pot and the plant stays; throw the pot away and the plant is gone.

Common interview traps.

  • Creating a heavy object in init of a view; it may be built repeatedly and thrown away.
  • Starting Task { } in onAppear without cancelling it on disappear.
  • Assuming there is a ViewModel store that survives navigation pop (there is not).
  • Android vs iOS: rotation does not recreate state; process death does, and nothing is auto-restored unless you wire it.

notes.title: Common state bugs and fixes
notes.html:
Android equivalent first. Compose's equivalents are "state reads in the wrong scope", "unstable parameters causing excessive recomposition" and "remember without key". SwiftUI has its own set.

Symptom Likely cause Fix
State resets to initial on parent update View identity changed (if/else swap, .id changes, ForEach id unstable) Keep branch structure stable; use stable ids; use parameterised modifiers
Text field loses focus/text after each keystroke Parent rebuilds child with new identity, or model recreated each render Stable id; own the model with @State/@StateObject
UI does not refresh after mutating an object Plain class stored in @State/let (no observation) Make class @Observable, or use a struct
Everything re-renders on any change Legacy ObservableObject with many @Published; or one giant model passed to every child Migrate to @Observable; pass narrow inputs; split models
"Modifying state during view update" Writing state in body, in init, or in a computed property called from body Move to .onAppear / .task / action handlers
Crash "No Observable object of type X found" Missing .environment(model) Inject at the root; use optional environment read; fix sheet roots
Model recreated, data lost @ObservedObject var m = Model() or @State var m = Model() in a view that is itself recreated Create once in the owner at a stable position; inject to children
Stale closure data Closure captured an old value in Task Read from the model inside the task or use .task(id:)
Async mutates from background Missing @MainActor Mark model @MainActor; fix Swift 6 errors, do not silence them
onChange fires twice or on first load Initial value assigned in .onAppear causing a change Use onChange(of:initial:) (iOS 17) intentionally or guard
Binding to a computed array element crashes Binding outlives the row after deletion (index out of range) Use ForEach($items) element bindings; avoid $items[index] captured by long-lived closures

Example: state lost by conditional wrapper.

// Bug: toggling `isCompact` swaps the type and resets `ChatView` state
if isCompact { ChatView().padding() } else { ChatView() }

// Fix: same structural position, different modifier value
ChatView().padding(isCompact ? 8 : 0)

Example: over-invalidation.

// Bug: row reads the whole model, any change re-renders every row
struct Row: View { let model: AppModel; let id: Item.ID
  var body: some View { Text(model.items.first { $0.id == id }?.title ?? "") } }

// Fix: pass a value (Item) so the row depends only on its own data
struct Row: View { let item: Item
  var body: some View { Text(item.title) } }

State management at app scale. Beyond per-screen @Observable models: navigation state and flows in a router object (see navigation note), unidirectional stores (TCA, Redux-like), repository layer with SwiftData or networking, and dependency injection. This mirrors Android's MVVM/MVI + repository + Hilt stack, which is why Android developers usually find TCA similar to MVI libraries like Orbit or Mavericks (Airbnb's own Android framework).

Testing state. @Observable models are plain classes: unit test them with Swift Testing (@Test, #expect) with no UI. For view snapshots use swift-snapshot-testing. Use withObservationTracking to assert that changes notify.

import Testing

@MainActor
@Test func addingItemUpdatesTotal() {
    let model = CartModel()
    model.items = [CartItem(name: "Tea", price: 3)]
    #expect(model.total == 3)
}

Production incident patterns. (1) A paywall screen reappears after purchase because the entitlement flag lived in a view's @State that was reset when the parent swapped branches. (2) Battery drain and jank from an ObservableObject that publishes on every location update to a screen-wide object. (3) A crash after logout because environment models were force-read in views that remained on screen while the session was cleared; model "signed out" as a state, not as nil.

Real industry examples. Airbnb's Android Mavericks, TCA on iOS, Spotify's and Uber's internal architectures all push toward single-owner, explicit state; the bugs above are why.

Everyday analogy. Debugging state is tracing plumbing: find the one valve (source of truth) that really controls the tap, instead of turning every tap in the house.

Common interview traps.

  • Silencing "modifying state during view update" by wrapping in DispatchQueue.main.async instead of fixing the data flow.
  • Using @State for data that must outlive the screen.
  • Believing @Observable removes the need for stable identity; it does not.
  • Android vs iOS: SavedStateHandle has no automatic twin; plan restoration deliberately.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• Keep one source of truth. Local value: @State. Two-way pass-down: @Binding. Model with logic: @Observable class held in @State by its creator. Cross-tree dependency: @Environment. Small settings: @AppStorage. Window restoration: @SceneStorage.
  • @State storage lives outside the struct and is tied to view identity; the initial value is applied once; it is destroyed when the identity leaves the tree.
  • @Observable tracks per-property reads in body, so only dependent views update; ObservableObject invalidates all observers and uses @StateObject/@ObservedObject (legacy).
  • @Bindable gives $ bindings to model properties; @Environment(Type.self) injects models (crashes if missing); custom keys use @Entry (verify) or EnvironmentKey with a static let default.
  • @AppStorage is UserDefaults for small non-secret values (use App Groups for widgets); @SceneStorage is restoration only, not a database.
  • SwiftUI invalidates the attribute graph, re-evaluates dependent bodys, diffs and updates only changed output; closures as inputs defeat skipping; use _printChanges and Instruments.
  • Use .task/.task(id:) for async loads, scenePhase for foreground/background, and avoid heavy inits.
  • Most state bugs are identity changes, plain-class mutation, state writes in body, missing environment injection, and over-wide model dependencies; test models with Swift Testing.
